transcript:
[00:00] Ana Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining the Redwood x BrightWave chat, we'll do a conversational interview today for about 50 minutes, record's on.
[00:12] Samantha Ortiz: Great, excited, thanks for having us.
[00:16] Marcus Li: Quick mic check, all good.
[00:20] Jordan Kim: Awesome. Uh Samantha, maybe start with a little background—what were you trying to solve with LLMs at BrightWave?
[00:31] Samantha Ortiz: Yeah sure, so we had this push to add generative features into our content creation pipeline, right. Our product teams were experimenting with a couple of hosted APis, um OpenAI mainly, and we hit a bunch of friction when we tried to scale—latency ani and cost, and also security for certain enterprise customers.
[00:52] Evan Carter: To add, we also needed deterministic performance for live editing features; customers expect <pause> instant-ish responses, not a five second lag.
[01:03] Marcus Li: When you say latency, what were typical numbers before Redwood?
[01:07] Evan Carter: For our median path it was around 1.1 to 1.4 seconds per response for short prompts; tail p95s hit 2.8s during spikes, which was painful in the editor experience.
[01:18] Ana Patel: And after moving to Redwood Dedicated?
[01:21] Samantha Ortiz: We saw medians down to about 300ms on typical prompts, p95 around 600-800ms. Cost per active user token spend dropped by about 35-45% — that was a big part of the business case.
[01:35] Jordan Kim: Those are great numbers—can you walk us through why Redwood helped with both latency and cost?
[01:42] Samantha Ortiz: Sure. A few things: dedicated GPU pools meant we didn't share noisy neighbors with other tenants, continuous batching plus KV cache improved throughput, and we tuned quant profiles per model to balance cost and quality. Marcus and the SE team were super helpful translating our workloads to the right model variant.
[02:00] Marcus Li: We also suggested prefix caching for common prompts and a smaller context window for the live editor which saved tokens.
[02:08] Evan Carter: Right—those engineering changes plus the runtime optimizations resulted in both lower latency and lower token costs.
[02:15] Samantha Ortiz: And the rollout tools—canary deploys and automatic fallback—gave us confidence to test model updates without taking the editor offline.
[02:24] Jordan Kim: Great. On security and compliance, a few of our readers will want specifics. BrightWave had strict requirements — what did you validate?
[02:33] Samantha Ortiz: We needed private networking, so the Redwood Private VPC deployment was key. We integrated with our KMS for key management, enforced RBAC, SAML SSO for team access, and audited logs—helped with SOC 2 readiness. There was a small hiccup with the initial SSO mapping but Marcus' team fixed the SAML roles mapping in the first week.
[02:57] Evan Carter: The audit logs were especially useful for our security reviews; being able to hand an export to the compliance team was huge.
[03:06] Ana Patel: There was a point early on where BrightWave considered staying on Vertex/Anthropic for simplicity—what tipped the scales?
[03:14] Samantha Ortiz: It was a combo: performance guarantees from Dedicated plus the cost modeling Redwood showed, and the ability to run in our VPC. Also the early benchmark RPC that Marcus ran matched our production prompts more closely than the public examples. That helped the execs feel comfortable.
[03:32] Marcus Li: Yeah we ran a short benchmark using their typical prompt set and sequence length distribution—results were close to their production distribution which made the forecasts reliable.
[03:41] Jordan Kim: Samantha, can you share a short anecdote about a moment where Redwood saved the day?
[03:45] Samantha Ortiz: Uh, yeah — during a holiday campaign we had 3x usual traffic and the editor latency spiked with the previous provider. With Redwood Dedicated we were able to autoscale and also hit the fallback policy to a slightly cheaper model variant for non-critical routes, so the live editor stayed responsive and we avoided rolling back the feature. The campaign converted 2.4x higher than baseline, so it was important.
[04:10] Evan Carter: That was a big win—the ability to define routing policies by route and cost was one of those operational levers we hadn't had before.
[04:18] Ana Patel: Did you run into any issues on onboarding? Time to first meaningful test?
[04:22] Samantha Ortiz: Initial setup took longer than we hoped because of internal network approvals, but once the VPC was allowed and the KMS keys were set up, getting a canary running took about a week. Marcus' docs and post-call notes were really helpful.
[04:36] Marcus Li: We try to provide a checklist for the infra teams; sometimes firewall rules and egress need extra ops time.
[04:41] Jordan Kim: For the case study headline—Samantha, what's the one metric you'd want us to highlight?
[04:47] Samantha Ortiz: Latency improvements for the editor and the cost reduction—maybe lead with "Editor latency cut ~70% and token costs down ~40%".
[04:56] Ana Patel: Nice. We'll also capture the migration timeline and the VPC/KMS security bit in the body.
[05:02] Samantha Ortiz: And please use our logo and a short quote: "Redwood made inference predictable and affordable at scale"—I'll send the approved version.
[05:12] Jordan Kim: Perfect — Lina, any thoughts on distribution?
[05:15] Lina Gomez: We can syndicate the podcast episode on our channels and Redwood's channels; short clips for LinkedIn and a blog post. We also want a joint webinar later this quarter.
[05:26] Ana Patel: Great, we'll coordinate.
[05:28] Marcus Li: Quick technical Q — Evan, were you able to use the model variant suggestions without changing the editor UX?
[05:34] Evan Carter: Yeah, Marcus' team provided a transparent fallback that downgraded complexity only on non-blocking routes, users didn't notice.
[05:41] Jordan Kim: Any callouts about competitor features?
[05:44] Samantha Ortiz: Some providers had nicer hosted sample models, but they lacked the cost controls and private deployment options we needed. Also, vendor lock-in risk was a conversation.
[05:55] Ana Patel: Okay let's wrap up with the promotional ask — are you comfortable with the audio being edited and snippets used in marketing?
[06:02] Samantha Ortiz: Yes, happy for that. We'll review the final draft of the case study.
[06:07] Jordan Kim: Awesome. Final recap of next steps: Redwood to send edited audio and transcript; marketing to draft case study and send to BrightWave; Samantha to provide logo and testimonial.
[06:18] Ana Patel: Thanks so much, everyone. Appreciate the time.
[06:22] Samantha Ortiz: Thanks—looking forward to it.
[06:25] [END RECORDING]

Note: transcription contains occasional mis-hear and filler words; timestamps approximate. Shared artifacts referenced during call: link to benchmark spreadsheet (internal), draft case study (to be shared), SSO/KMS integration notes (internal).
